title: I’m stuck: Is this a Visual Novel or an Interactive Movie? What am I doing wrong?
author: KDH_Studio_Official
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I’m an architect by trade, building a dystopian project called "FLATLINE: pay to feel" solo (using Tuesday JS and AI for environment design).

I recently launched a demo on Steam, positioning it as a Visual Novel. But the traffic completely bypassed me. Now I’m thinking about shifting it to the "Interactive Movie" category, but I'm honestly lost.

The core loop: It’s a gritty story about London 2036 where a virus wiped out human emotions, and you literally have to buy synthetic feelings from the government (BHS) to survive catatonia. Nature reclaims the city because people became too numb to care. Your choices dictate your emotional resource management.

Here is the YouTube teaser to show the atmosphere and visual style.

[YouTube FLATLINE teaser](https://youtu.be/a4Rfa_8ZS0c)

Based on the footage, what genre does this look like to you? VN or Interactive Movie? What am I missing here?

[Steam FLATLINE Demo](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4711800/FLATLINE_Pay_to_Feel/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social)

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body: What do you mean the traffic “completely bypassed you”? Most games do not get traffic from posting demos on Steam. The traffic has to come from somewhere.

replies.author: KDH_Studio_Official
replies.body:
You're absolutely right, traffic doesn’t just appear out of thin air. 

What I meant is that I'm currently stuck in a 'grey zone' with only 85 wishlists after 3 weeks since the demo release, which is honestly a bit discouraging for a solo dev.
To add some context, the game actually participated in the recent Steam Cyberpunk Fest. I had high hopes, but it didn't generate any significant spike in traffic or wishlists.

Looking back, I feel like my initial choice of the 'Visual Novel' tag completely mismatched what the core VN audience expects (they usually look for romance or specific art tropes). 
My game is much more focused on environmental storytelling, cinematic pacing, and psychological resource management. 
By using the wrong genre tag during the festival, I think I completely choked whatever organic impressions Steam tried to give me.

But then again, as an architect who is completely new to game marketing, I might be completely missing something here. Would love to hear your thoughts!

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
I think you should evaluate the alternative explanations as well, not just the “mistagged” explanation:

\* The right people haven’t seen your trailer, but tagging the game isn’t enough

\* Your game is good and the market exists, but there is something wrong with the trailer

\* Your game is good but the market is small

\* Your game isn’t that good

It can be discouraging. That’s why I suggest making more games and not getting attached to the success or failure of any one game, especially if it’s your first game.

replies.author: KDH_Studio_Official
replies.body:
This is a harsh but incredibly necessary reality check.. Thank you!,

When you're solo and deep into development, it's very easy to develop tunnel vision.
Your breakdown makes total sense, but there is one crucial detail: the trailer is mostly there just to show off the visual style. The actual gameplay and the demo tell a completely different story. The engagement metric is great — when a player actually downloads and launches the demo, they play it all the way through to the end. The core game loop works.That’s why, since I already have enough narrative material and motivation, my plan is to finish and launch the Pilot Episode anyway.

 I need to get this build out to the public and gather real player data from an actual release before I can say: 'Okay, we gathered the experience, let's move on to the next project.'

But looking at the storefront from the outside — what was your immediate reaction to the trailer or the page? If the gameplay itself holds players until the end, what do you think is stopping people from clicking that 'Download Demo' button in the first place?

 I'm completely open to brutal honesty.😉

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: I don’t know what the game is like from the trailer. I have no idea what kind of gameplay it has.

replies.author: KDH_Studio_Official
replies.body:
You just hit the exact bottleneck....!! 

And the hard data from Steamworks completely backs up your point.I just checked the deeper analytics, and the funnel looks like this: the demo got over 1,000 total downloads (mostly during festivals). But out of those 1,000 people, only 65 players actually launched it...! 

But here is the crazy part: the average playtime for those 65 people is around 6 minutes — which is the exact full length of the entire demo. 

This means almost every single person who actually opens the game plays it cover to cover until the final credits. The game loop works, but the 'storefront wrap' fails to explain what the game actually is.

I made a trailer that focuses entirely on architectural atmosphere and cinematic mood, completely hiding the gameplay mechanics (BHS system, emotional resource management, choices). People download it based on the vibe, but then it sits dead in their libraries because they don't know what they are supposed to Do in it.

Lesson absolutely learned for the Pilot Episode. I need a trailer that actually shows the UI, the choices, and how the game is played, not just pretty post-pandemic landscapes. 

Thank you for opening my eyes to this!
